overview: This approved research collection contains 117 publications: 51 randomized controlled trial reports, 25 reviews or meta-analyses, and 41 other studies. These are publication counts, not independent trials or participants. Selected approaches include 10 EMDR publications, 9 on mindfulness or meditation, and 8 on music-based approaches; these groups overlap and do not cover every approach.
limitations: AI assessed; human approved for publication. These are research summaries, not personal treatment recommendations. Evidence was assessed from 74 abstracts, 22 selected-methods sources and 21 retained full-text appraisals. No double-blind trial is verified. Benefits, null results, harms-reporting gaps and population limits remain attached to each paper.

records.design: Randomized controlled feasibility study with material allocation-protocol deviations
records.finding: PST-IPV was implementable with adaptations, but serious allocation errors, 25% missing follow-up and short descriptive assessment preclude an efficacy conclusion. One serious assault event was reported without arm or causal attribution.
records.summary: PST-IPV was implementable with adaptations, but serious allocation errors, 25% missing follow-up and short descriptive assessment preclude an efficacy conclusion. One serious assault event was reported without arm or causal attribution.
records.limitation: Seventeen women with psychological/emotional IPV had no chance of assignment toPST-IPV; baseline imbalance suggests possible nonrandom allocation. Twelve of 39 assessments occurred before 9 weeks. Underpowered feasibility, missing follow-up, provider fidelity problems and overlapping IPV recall periods limit interpretation.

evidence.evidenceType: Randomized controlled feasibility study with material allocation-protocol deviations
evidence.intervention: Four-session problem-solving therapy adapted with trauma/IPV-informed training, risk awareness and avoidance of victim blaming; sessions address participants’ chosen problems. Four sessions within 8 weeks; mean session durations approximately 32–51 minutes. 19/25 completed all 4; 5 attended none, 1 attended one.
evidence.comparator: Four-session standard PST (12 women) or enhanced usual care (15 women: well-being leaflet and local support information). All arms additional to routine antenatal care. Shared comparator structure with linked depression feasibility trial.

records.finding: Nguvu was feasible for some refugee women, but the adjusted randomized comparison does not clearly establish psychological or IPV benefit. Severe IPV predicted lower completion; an exploratory subgroup showed higher subsequent IPV. No long-term durability was tested.
records.summary: Nguvu was feasible for some refugee women, but the adjusted randomized comparison does not clearly establish psychological or IPV benefit. Severe IPV predicted lower completion; an exploratory subgroup showed higher subsequent IPV. No long-term durability was tested.
records.limitation: Under-recruitment, baseline imbalances, recruitment after cluster assignment, unmasked self-report, vulnerable assessor masking, complete-case analysis and severity-related intervention dropout limit causal inference. Table 1 reverses the narrative cluster-arm counts; all 43 clusters and individual 158/153 totals are retained.

evidence.evidenceType: Cluster randomized feasibility trial with recruitment after cluster allocation
evidence.intervention: Nguvu integrates shortened cognitive processing therapy with advocacy counselling, adapted for refugee women. One individual plus seven weekly group sessions; groups 6–13, facilitated in pairs. Mean 5.4/8 attended; 92/158 (58.2%)completed≥6, 47/158 all 8, 13/158 none.
evidence.comparator: Information about existing protection/mental-health services and usual humanitarian case management/referrals; Nguvu participants could also access these services.
evidence.sample: 43 groups randomized before individual recruitment; 311 enrolled women assigned 158 Nguvu/153 usual care. Follow-up 275 (143/132); adjusted main model 272 and completer analysis 219. Target 400 was not achieved. Narrative and Table 1 reverse cluster-arm counts; retain 43 total and flag discrepancy.
evidence.measurement: Psychological distress: depression, anxiety, PTSD; Psychological, physical and sexual IPV frequency; Functional impairment; Exploratory high-baseline-IPV subgroup; PTSD among intervention completers
evidence.timing: Nine weeks after enrollment, approximately one week after intervention; Nine weeks
evidence.relationshipNote: Explicit domestic/intimate-partner violence exposure in the studied population; psychological intervention is within Language scope. See limitation and quality fields; no population-wide clinical recommendation is implied.

outcomes.name: Psychological distress: depression, anxiety, PTSD
outcomes.followUp: Nine weeks after enrollment, approximately one week after intervention
outcomes.result: Baseline-adjusted randomized complete-case estimates do not clearly exclude no benefit; apparent unadjusted differences attenuate.
outcomes.uncertainty: Cluster mixed models adjust demographics and baseline outcome imbalance; PTSD upperCI rounded to 0.00. Not evidence of a definitive efficacy effect.

outcomes.name: Psychological, physical and sexual IPV frequency
outcomes.result: No clear comparative benefit after baseline adjustment.
outcomes.effectEstimate: Log-frequency MD psychological 0.10 (95% CI−0.04, 0.24); physical 0.09 (−0.03, 0.21); sexual−0.03 (−0.24, 0.17).
outcomes.uncertainty: Positive values favor usual care; all intervals include zero. These are log-transformed frequency outcomes, not risk ratios.

outcomes.name: Functional impairment
outcomes.result: No clear comparative difference.

outcomes.name: Exploratory high-baseline-IPV subgroup
outcomes.result: Higher subsequent IPV frequency reported with Nguvu among women above the baseline IPV median.
outcomes.uncertainty: Underpowered moderator tests, multiple comparisons, baseline imbalance and differential completion; a signal to retain, not established treatment-caused harm.

outcomes.name: PTSD among intervention completers
outcomes.result: Selected completer analysis favored Nguvu; it must not replace the randomized comparison.
outcomes.uncertainty: Treatment completion associated with baseline IPV severity; per-protocol comparison is vulnerable to selection bias.

quality.riskOfBias: Important concerns from baseline mental-health/IPV imbalance, post-allocation recruitment, unmasked self-report and possible assessor unmasking; no formal numeric rating.
quality.attrition: 36/311 (11.6%) lacked endline: 15/158 Nguvu, 21/153 usual care. Eighteen relocated/resettled. Later resettlement stages predicted loss. One withdrew fearing neighbors would learn of participation. Intervention completion 92/158 is distinct from study follow-up 143/158.
quality.confounding: Models 1–3 labeled ITT by authors are complete-case randomized-group comparisons, not all 311 participants. Model 3 controls baseline imbalances; favorable per-protocol PTSD estimate is selected. Moderator tests are exploratory, multiple and underpowered.
quality.adverseFindings: Three adverse events reviewed by DSMB/IRB were judged unlikely due to participation and consistent with ongoing IPV; participants were connected to services. Exploratory high-baseline-IPV group had higher subsequent IPV frequency with Nguvu; not causal proof. One privacy-related withdrawal.
quality.transferLimits: Adult Congolese women in established refugee groups with past-year physical/sexual IPV and elevated distress. Imminent suicidality/severe psychiatric impairment excluded; no durability beyond nine weeks.

maskingRoles.assessors: Not informed of allocation, but familiar with Nguvu and could infer it from participants at endline; integrity not established.

outcomes.name: Psychological distress: depression, anxiety, PTSD

outcomes.result: Baseline-adjusted randomized complete-case estimates do not clearly exclude no benefit; apparent unadjusted differences attenuate.

outcomes.name: Psychological, physical and sexual IPV frequency

outcomes.name: Functional impairment
outcomes.result: No clear comparative difference.

outcomes.name: Exploratory high-baseline-IPV subgroup

outcomes.name: PTSD among intervention completers

outcomes.name: CAPS PTSD severity and IPV measures
outcomes.result: Both active arms improved, but no significant between-group difference at any occasion or in change from baseline.
outcomes.effectEstimate: Reported absolute between-group standardized differences≤0.32 at occasions and≤0.30 for change; no comparative confidence interval provided in the main-report results.
outcomes.uncertainty: No inactive control; null superiority tests do not establish equivalence or isolate therapy from shelter/time effects.

outcomes.name: Reliable PTSD improvement and diagnosis
outcomes.result: Post-treatment reliable CAPS improvement 54/65 (83.1%)HOPE versus 59/77 (76.6%)PCT+; group difference not significant. PTSD diagnosis rates also did not significantly differ at follow-up.
outcomes.uncertainty: These are assessed-participant denominators, not 172 randomized participants.

outcomes.name: Depression, empowerment, posttraumatic cognitions and health-related quality of life
outcomes.result: Within-group improvements without significant comparative superiority.
outcomes.uncertainty: Some residual depression, subthreshold PTSD and abuse remained. Multiple comparisons used alpha<.01.

quality.riskOfBias: Randomization and masked clinical assessment strengthen comparison. Therapist allegiance/performance effects, possible contamination, unverified participant-role masking and follow-up attrition remain. No formal RoB or Jadad score assigned.

records.finding: At 24 months the WEAVE counselling offer did not improve primary or secondary outcomes versus usual care. The 12-month secondary depression finding did not persist; these reports are one cohort.
records.summary: At 24 months the WEAVE counselling offer did not improve primary or secondary outcomes versus usual care. The 12-month secondary depression finding did not persist; these reports are one cohort.
records.limitation: Only 166/272 responded at 24 months and 49% of women offered counselling attended any (mostlyone session). Self-reported outcomes were unmasked. The absence of statistical benefit is not equivalence; within-group improvement does not establish counselling efficacy.

evidence.intervention: Woman-centered family-doctor counselling using active listening, motivational interviewing and problem solving, supporting the woman’s readiness and decisions. Offered 1–6 free sessions over 6 months. 67/137 (49%)attended any; most attended one. Doctor training 6 hours distance learning plus 1 hour practice visit.
evidence.comparator: Usual primary care; both groups’ doctors received basic IPV information and women received resource lists.
evidence.sample: Same 52 doctor-cluster cohort as 2013; 24-month respondents 81/137 intervention and 85/135 control. Longitudinal models used available data for all baseline participants, so 166 is final time point count, not a new trial.
evidence.measurement: SF-12 mental health and quality of life; Depression, anxiety, PTSD and IPV caseness; Physical health; Participant-reported benefit/harm

quality.riskOfBias: Unmasked self-report, low counselling uptake, substantial long-term attrition and selected English-speaking screening responders limit inference. Masked researchers/analysts and cluster-adjusted analyses support methods; no formal numerical risk rating.

quality.confounding: Mixed-effects models use available repeated observations, adjusted for practice clustering and urban/rural stratification. Nonattender exclusions are selected analyses. Both arms received information/resources and repeated IPV questionnaires.
quality.adverseFindings: Report says no significant harms detected and refers to the dedicated harms analysis. A same-family primary abstract nevertheless describes short-/long-term negative emotions, recall, retraumatization and minimization. agePopulation.reportedAges: Not established from the inspected source sections.

records.design: Secondary meta-regression of previously reviewed intervention studies
records.finding: The analysis relates study-average baseline violence patterns and treatment components to pre/post changes. It cannot establish which component works for an individual or prove superiority between treatments.
records.summary: The analysis relates study-average baseline violence patterns and treatment components to pre/post changes. It cannot establish which component works for an individual or prove superiority between treatments.
records.limitation: Ecological associations, uncontrolled change scores, heterogeneous programmes and imputation limit inference. Missing predictors were imputed with k-nearest neighbors (k=5); narrative study-flow arithmetic and sexual-violence study totals are inconsistent, so exact subsidiary counts and treatment rankings are not adopted.

evidence.evidenceType: Secondary meta-regression of previously reviewed intervention studies
evidence.intervention: Study-level combinations of CBT, substance-use treatment, motivational work and other perpetrator programme components. Varied by source study; no shared regimen.

evidence.sample: 16 studies reused from Karakurt et al. 2019; no new eligible studies added by the update search. Participant total not established in this assessment.
evidence.measurement: Physical, psychological and sexual IPV change; Variance change
evidence.relationshipNote: Adds a methodological audit of a previously included evidence base; it is not new independent trial evidence or a basis for individualized treatment ranking. Ecological associations, uncontrolled change scores, heterogeneous programmes and imputation limit inference. Missing predictors were imputed with k-nearest neighbors (k=5); narrative study-flow arithmetic and sexual-violence study totals are inconsistent, so exact subsidiary counts and treatment rankings are not adopted.

language.title: AI Guided Recommendations
overview: This approved research collection contains 117 publications: 51 randomized controlled trial reports, 25 reviews or meta-analyses, and 41 other studies. These are publication counts, not independent trials or participants. Selected approaches include 10 EMDR publications, 9 on mindfulness or meditation, and 8 on music-based approaches; these groups overlap and do not cover every approach.

AI assessed; human approved for publication. These are research summaries, not personal treatment recommendations. Evidence was assessed from 74 abstracts, 22 selected-methods sources and 21 retained full-text appraisals. No double-blind trial is verified. Benefits, null results, harms-reporting gaps and population limits remain attached to each paper.

outcomes.result: 19/25 PST-IPV and 8/12 standard PST completed all 4 sessions. Providers sometimes ignored IPV disclosures; risk/confidentiality discussion needed improvement.

outcomes.result: One serious adverse event: assault by husband. Two obstructed/prolonged-labour complications among 29 participants who had delivered.

papers.finding: Nguvu was feasible for some refugee women, but the adjusted randomized comparison does not clearly establish psychological or IPV benefit. Severe IPV predicted lower completion; an exploratory subgroup showed higher subsequent IPV. No long-term durability was tested.
papers.summary: Nguvu was feasible for some refugee women, but the adjusted randomized comparison does not clearly establish psychological or IPV benefit. Severe IPV predicted lower completion; an exploratory subgroup showed higher subsequent IPV. No long-term durability was tested.
papers.limitation: Under-recruitment, baseline imbalances, recruitment after cluster assignment, unmasked self-report, vulnerable assessor masking, complete-case analysis and severity-related intervention dropout limit causal inference. Table 1 reverses the narrative cluster-arm counts; all 43 clusters and individual 158/153 totals are retained.

evidence.evidenceType: Cluster randomized feasibility trial with recruitment after cluster allocation
evidence.intervention: Nguvu integrates shortened cognitive processing therapy with advocacy counselling, adapted for refugee women. One individual plus seven weekly group sessions; groups 6–13, facilitated in pairs. Mean 5.4/8 attended; 92/158 (58.2%)completed≥6, 47/158 all 8, 13/158 none.
evidence.comparator: Information about existing protection/mental-health services and usual humanitarian case management/referrals; Nguvu participants could also access these services.
evidence.sample: 43 groups randomized before individual recruitment; 311 enrolled women assigned 158 Nguvu/153 usual care. Follow-up 275 (143/132); adjusted main model 272 and completer analysis 219. Target 400 was not achieved. Narrative and Table 1 reverse cluster-arm counts; retain 43 total and flag discrepancy.
evidence.measurement: Psychological distress: depression, anxiety, PTSD; Psychological, physical and sexual IPV frequency; Functional impairment; Exploratory high-baseline-IPV subgroup; PTSD among intervention completers

outcomes.name: Psychological distress: depression, anxiety, PTSD
outcomes.followUp: Nine weeks after enrollment, approximately one week after intervention
outcomes.result: Baseline-adjusted randomized complete-case estimates do not clearly exclude no benefit; apparent unadjusted differences attenuate.
outcomes.uncertainty: Cluster mixed models adjust demographics and baseline outcome imbalance; PTSD upperCI rounded to 0.00. Not evidence of a definitive efficacy effect.

outcomes.name: Psychological, physical and sexual IPV frequency
outcomes.result: No clear comparative benefit after baseline adjustment.
outcomes.effectEstimate: Log-frequency MD psychological 0.10 (95% CI−0.04, 0.24); physical 0.09 (−0.03, 0.21); sexual−0.03 (−0.24, 0.17).
outcomes.uncertainty: Positive values favor usual care; all intervals include zero. These are log-transformed frequency outcomes, not risk ratios.

outcomes.name: Functional impairment
outcomes.result: No clear comparative difference.

outcomes.name: Exploratory high-baseline-IPV subgroup
outcomes.result: Higher subsequent IPV frequency reported with Nguvu among women above the baseline IPV median.
outcomes.uncertainty: Underpowered moderator tests, multiple comparisons, baseline imbalance and differential completion; a signal to retain, not established treatment-caused harm.

outcomes.name: PTSD among intervention completers
outcomes.result: Selected completer analysis favored Nguvu; it must not replace the randomized comparison.
outcomes.uncertainty: Treatment completion associated with baseline IPV severity; per-protocol comparison is vulnerable to selection bias.

quality.riskOfBias: Important concerns from baseline mental-health/IPV imbalance, post-allocation recruitment, unmasked self-report and possible assessor unmasking; no formal numeric rating.
quality.attrition: 36/311 (11.6%) lacked endline: 15/158 Nguvu, 21/153 usual care. Eighteen relocated/resettled. Later resettlement stages predicted loss. One withdrew fearing neighbors would learn of participation. Intervention completion 92/158 is distinct from study follow-up 143/158.
quality.confounding: Models 1–3 labeled ITT by authors are complete-case randomized-group comparisons, not all 311 participants. Model 3 controls baseline imbalances; favorable per-protocol PTSD estimate is selected. Moderator tests are exploratory, multiple and underpowered.
quality.adverseFindings: Three adverse events reviewed by DSMB/IRB were judged unlikely due to participation and consistent with ongoing IPV; participants were connected to services. Exploratory high-baseline-IPV group had higher subsequent IPV frequency with Nguvu; not causal proof. One privacy-related withdrawal.
quality.transferLimits: Adult Congolese women in established refugee groups with past-year physical/sexual IPV and elevated distress. Imminent suicidality/severe psychiatric impairment excluded; no durability beyond nine weeks.

papers.finding: HOPE did not outperform an attention-matched PCT+ intervention on PTSD, IPV or secondary outcomes. Both active groups improved; no untreated control supports an absolute treatment-effect estimate.
papers.summary: HOPE did not outperform an attention-matched PCT+ intervention on PTSD, IPV or secondary outcomes. Both active groups improved; no untreated control supports an absolute treatment-effect estimate.
papers.limitation: Treatment providers knew protocols, and shared shelters permit contamination. Participant masking identity is not explicitly role-confirmed despite double-blind labeling. Missing-at-random models assume an unproven missingness mechanism; only 127/172 remained at 12 months. Active-comparator null results are not equivalence evidence.

evidence.evidenceType: Randomized active-comparator trial; author describes double-blind, but only assessor masking is explicitly role-verified
evidence.intervention: Empowerment-oriented, present-centered CBT with safety planning, cognitive restructuring and coping/relationship skills; current symptoms are linked to IPV but traumatic memories are not processed. Up to 16 sessions of 50–60 minutes during shelter and first 3 months after leaving; HOPE mean 8.86 sessions (SD 6.17), 44.2% attended at least 8. Eleven participants across arms received optional shelter boosters.
evidence.comparator: Attention-matched PCT+ with present-focused problem solving, psychoeducation and safety planning, up to 16 sessions; mean 10.06 (SD 5.82). Both groups also received standard shelter services.
evidence.sample: HOPE 83 versus PCT+ 89. ITT models use all available observations, not complete follow-up for 172. Follow-up counts 154, 142, 135, 127 at post-shelter, post-treatment, 6 and 12 months; outcome-specific denominators vary.
evidence.measurement: CAPS PTSD severity and IPV measures; Reliable PTSD improvement and diagnosis; Depression, empowerment, posttraumatic cognitions and health-related quality of life
evidence.timing: Post-shelter, post-treatment, 6 and 12 months; Post-treatment and later follow-up; Through 12 months post-treatment
evidence.relationshipNote: Explicit domestic/intimate-partner violence exposure in the studied population; psychological intervention is within Language scope. See limitation and quality fields; no population-wide clinical recommendation is implied.

outcomes.name: CAPS PTSD severity and IPV measures
outcomes.result: Both active arms improved, but no significant between-group difference at any occasion or in change from baseline.
outcomes.effectEstimate: Reported absolute between-group standardized differences≤0.32 at occasions and≤0.30 for change; no comparative confidence interval provided in the main-report results.
outcomes.uncertainty: No inactive control; null superiority tests do not establish equivalence or isolate therapy from shelter/time effects.

outcomes.name: Reliable PTSD improvement and diagnosis
outcomes.result: Post-treatment reliable CAPS improvement 54/65 (83.1%)HOPE versus 59/77 (76.6%)PCT+; group difference not significant. PTSD diagnosis rates also did not significantly differ at follow-up.
outcomes.uncertainty: These are assessed-participant denominators, not 172 randomized participants.

outcomes.name: Depression, empowerment, posttraumatic cognitions and health-related quality of life
outcomes.result: Within-group improvements without significant comparative superiority.
outcomes.uncertainty: Some residual depression, subthreshold PTSD and abuse remained. Multiple comparisons used alpha<.01.

quality.riskOfBias: Randomization and masked clinical assessment strengthen comparison. Therapist allegiance/performance effects, possible contamination, unverified participant-role masking and follow-up attrition remain. No formal RoB or Jadad score assigned.
quality.attrition: Assessment retention 154/172 post-shelter, 142/172 post-treatment, 135/172 at 6 months, 127/172 at 12 months. At 12 months 56/83 HOPE and 71/89 PCT+ contributed CAPS data. Treatment dropout 6/83 versus 5/89 is distinct from missing assessments. Black participants more often completed all assessments than White participants (81.6% vs 62.5%, p=.008).
quality.confounding: ITT multivariate models use all available data under missing-at-random assumption; robust SEs and alpha<.01. Significant within-group change cannot separate psychotherapy, shelter services and time.
quality.adverseFindings: Authors report no study-related serious adverse events, not zero adverse events overall. Ten participants were removed from assigned treatment for higher/different care: 6 HOPE, 4 PCT+; still invited to follow-up. Residual symptoms and some further abuse persisted.
quality.transferLimits: Women with recent IPV and diagnosed PTSD in US shelters; severe suicidal intent/plan, current psychosis, recent substance dependence, bipolar disorder or concurrent individual therapy were excluded.
